title: Can parts of my body other than my tongue sense bitter things?
blurb: Scientists made bitter-sensing cells glow green in mice. They found them in the windpipe and the stomach, not just on the tongue.

cover.alt: Microscope pictures of the tongue and the windpipe of a mouse, with a few cells glowing bright green.
cover.credit: Figure 2, Liu and Atzberger, Frontiers for Young Minds, CC BY 4.0

source.name: Frontiers for Young Minds
source.title: Can a Bitter Taste be Detected Outside the Tongue?
source.authors: Shuya Liu and Ann Kathleen Atzberger

original.title: Members of bitter taste receptor cluster Tas2r143/Tas2r135/Tas2r126 are expressed in the epithelium of murine airways and other non-gustatory tissues
original.authors: Liu, S., Lu, S., Xu, R., Atzberger, A., Günther, S., Wettschureck, N., et al.

cards.b: You taste with your tongue. It can sense five tastes: sweet, sour, salty, savoury and bitter. Bitter is the taste of things like bitter gourd, and it often warns us that a food may be harmful. The tongue senses bitter with tiny detectors called receptors. So scientists asked: are bitter receptors only on the tongue, or in other parts of the body too?

Shuya Liu and Ann Kathleen Atzberger worked with their team at the Max Planck Institute in Bad Nauheim, Germany. Shuya studied the heart and blood vessels. Ann runs a lab that finds and sorts different kinds of cells. The team published this study in 2017.

Receptors are far too small to see. So the team bred special mice. In these mice, any cell with one of three kinds of bitter receptor glows green. The team looked at many parts of the body under a microscope that shows glowing cells. A machine also picked out the green cells, one by one, so the team could study them.

img.alt: A drawing of a mouse whose bitter-sensing cells have been made to glow green.
img.credit: Figure 1, Liu and Atzberger, Frontiers for Young Minds, CC BY 4.0

cards.b: Green cells showed up on the tongue, as expected. They also showed up in the windpipe, the stomach and the urethra, the tube that carries urine out of the body. There were only a few cells in each place. All these places touch things from outside, like germs and dust. The green cells also held lots of a chemical message called IL-25.

img.alt: Microscope pictures of the tongue and the windpipe of a mouse, with a few cells glowing bright green.
img.credit: Figure 2, Liu and Atzberger, Frontiers for Young Minds, CC BY 4.0

cards.b: This study was in mice, not people. The team saw where the cells are, but not yet exactly what they do. Their best guess is that these cells notice germs and call the immune system, the body's defence team, for help. One clue fits: nobody tastes anything with their stomach, so bitter receptors there probably do a different job.

Here is why IL-25 matters. In the gut, cells like these release IL-25 when parasitic worms, small animals that live inside other bodies, move in. That starts a 'weep and sweep'. The gut makes more fluid, and squeezes harder, to wash the worms out. So bitter receptors may help the body spot invaders early and protect itself.

img.alt: A drawing of the idea: a germ touches a bitter-sensing cell, and the cell sends signals that call immune cells.
img.credit: Figure 3, Liu and Atzberger, Frontiers for Young Minds, CC BY 4.0

cards.b: Bitter is often a warning, but not always. Put five small tastes on a steel plate: bitter gourd, cocoa powder, cold green tea, a pinch of sugar and a pinch of salt. Taste each one, with a sip of water in between. Which are bitter? Which bitter ones are still good food? You will find that bitter is a signal to notice, not always a danger.

The body seems to use the same detector for two jobs: tasting food in the mouth, and noticing germs elsewhere. Which came first? Did bodies first use bitter receptors to notice germs, and the tongue borrowed them later for tasting? Or was it the other way round? What clue would help you decide? Talk about it, then pick an answer.

words.m: a tiny detector on the outside of a cell
a small group of taste cells on the tongue
the body's defence team against germs
a germ, like some bacteria or parasitic worms, that can cause illness
glowing brightly under a special light
